extracted.intended_audience: readers of an early-18th-century periodical (gentlemen and ladies interested in manners, letter-writing, and social conduct)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive periodical-essay guidance on social conduct, letter-writing, upbringing, wit vs. criticism, and practices (duels, dress, company) intended for a literate early-18th-century audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic should not be a perpetual censor
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic becomes the silliest of mortals by inuring himself to examine all things and viewing everything with a design of passing sentence upon it; thus he is never a companion but always a censor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making judgment the default posture toward all conversation and objects; do not turn social interaction into continual condemnation. Anti-pattern: always disputing indifferent matters with vehemence, standing 'in safety' but gaining no glory. Example figures: Spondee (the dull critic) contrasted with lively company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit must arise from occasion, not be premeditated
rubrics_metrics.description: A professional 'wit' who invents occasions to bring in his turns of phrase fails: what he says has an occasion invented to bring it in rather than arising from the occasion itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let wit flow naturally from dialogue and context; avoid premeditated turns that continue regardless of others' speech. Anti-pattern: the premeditated raconteur (e.g., Jasper Dactyle) who launches a prepared 'turn' and ignores the interlocutor, making responses pointless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good criticism requires genuine judgment, not mere citation or display
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'thorough critic' is like an intellectual puritan who cannot speak or write without citing celebrated authorities; over-reliance on authorities substitutes for real judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise independent judgment rather than bolstering opinions solely with named authorities. Anti-pattern: using famous writers as a crutch to excuse hesitations or errors ('Mr. Dryden makes such a character on such an occasion break off...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Write letters as near to how you would speak face-to-face
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no rule for writing letters except to be as near what you would speak face to face as you can; writing that exaggerates complaint or tender dependence often fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep letter tone conversational and proportionate; avoid excessive plaintiveness or showing that your entire life depends on the addressee. Example contrast: Careless's negligent, lively letter vs. Constant's solemn, self-sacrificing epistle; the livelier, companionable letter more often wins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divert your mistress; pleasantness prevails over languishing lament
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, divert your mistress rather than sigh to her: the pleasant man she will desire for his own sake; the languishing lover only hopes for her pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the tone of a companion and a lively presence rather than mournful adoration. Concrete example: Romana values the lively, negligent Careless over the tragic Constant despite Constant's nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe children's temper and inclinations and educate accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the temper and inclinations of childhood and youth so as not to give vice and folly supplies from the growing generation; put children to what they are fit or unfit for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign roles and education based on natural tendencies: a plodding, provident boy should be trained for commerce/citizenship; an arrogant bright boy may be sent to college where ridicule will correct coxcombry; a subtle, retiring child might be placed in courtly service to learn manners. Examples: three nephews assigned different futures (citizen, Oxford, page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding (manners) often outweighs learning for social success
rubrics_metrics.description: A good mien in court will carry a man further than a good understanding elsewhere; wisdom, valour, justice, and learning cannot keep a man in countenance if he lacks the art of life and behaviour called 'good breeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate manners and the social arts alongside (or even above) abstract learning if one seeks success in courtly and social settings. Analogy: a man with gold but no change for ordinary occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed conversation diminishes the effect of spoken wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The prettiest things said in company make a very small appearance when put into print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect the same reception for witticisms when transposed from immediate company to print; oral timing, delivery, and situation matter. Example: lively supper repartee loses sparkle when printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect dress codes and public decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Public notices admonish those who 'dress themselves as they please, without regard to decorum' (e.g., blue and red stockings in mourning; tucked cravats; nightcap wigs before people of the first quality) and demand compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to established norms of dress and decorum in appropriate settings or expect censure; anti-pattern: ostentatious or inappropriate mixing of mourning and bright colors, informal night attire in high company. Enforcement example: Mr. Bickerstaff's demand for compliance or removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent quarrels by measured arbitration and composed arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than resorting to single combat, employ measured assessment of affronts and argumentative remedies to prevent quarrelling; there exist 'set of arguments to be spoken to any man in a passion' which will prevent quarrelling if he listens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calm mediation and preformulated de-escalatory language to settle provocations; anti-pattern: rushing to duel or allowing heated words to determine honor. Context: Mr. Bickerstaff offers such arguments and will 'measure the degree of an affront' to avoid duels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor wit to its proper audience and local circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit must describe its proper circumference and not go beyond it; London wit does not necessarily travel, and attempts to export it may be 'bamboozling' to provincial audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the limits of your audience's references and tastes; local or topical wit may fail outside its social circle. Example: a country cousin who brought physical copies of the periodical around found no recognition or relish for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value substance and temper over mere briskness in company
rubrics_metrics.description: The prettiest company (the quick, brisk talker) may only have a knack of saying common things, whereas the quieter, sly, serious person can 'say home things enough' and be truly good company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer depth and well-timed replies to mere rapid brilliancy; cultivate a sly seriousness that lands meaningful repartee rather than constant light chatter. Example: contrast between Mistress Giddy (brisk but silly) and Mrs. Slim (less talkative but understanding).
